chapters.title: Chapter 6: Reporting and Getting It Right

lessons.title: Case Study: One Salaried Investor's Capital Gains Across Five Asset Classes

body.text: Everything in this course meets in one return. Five asset classes, five sets of rules, one taxpayer, and a final number that depends on classification, set-off, exemptions and the choices made before 31 March.

children.text: Aarav, a 38-year-old product manager in Pune, earns ₹18,00,000 of taxable salary and is in the new tax regime. During tax year 2026-27 he sold something from almost every asset class this course has covered. Work through his year with him, and you will have used every chapter.

body.caption: Aarav's transactions in tax year 2026-27 (all figures illustrative)

cells: Sold shares held 3 years, and a few held 5 months
Redeemed SIP units, some in profit and some in loss
Sold for ₹42,00,000 with 1% brokerage, invested ₹10,00,000 in section 85 bonds
Gain on Bitcoin, loss on Solana

children.text: Before any arithmetic, each gain has to be put in the right bucket, because that decides the rate. Two of Aarav's gains are not capital gains at the special rates at all, and one is not even a capital gain in the ordinary sense.

body.caption: The correct bucket for each item

cells: Shares held 3 years, equity fund units held over 12 months
Long-term at 12.5%, or 20% with indexation as a resident who bought before 23 July 2024
Flat 30%, no set-off of the Solana loss

body.title: Spot the Costly Miss
body.question: Which one of Aarav's decisions cost him the most in avoidable tax, purely on timing?
options: Selling shares held 5 months instead of waiting past 12 months
Selling US stocks after 14 months instead of waiting past 24 months
Redeeming the debt fund after two years instead of three
Selling the gold ETF at 20 months instead of 24
body.explanation: US stocks are foreign shares on the 24-month clock, so at 14 months his gain is short-term and taxed at his slab rate of 30% rather than 12.5%. Waiting would have more than halved that tax. The debt fund gain is short-term however long he holds, and the gold ETF was already long-term at 20 months because listed units use the 12-month clock.

children.text: His ₹25,000 short-term loss on equity fund units is the flexible kind, so he applies it against his ₹40,000 of short-term equity gains taxed at 20% rather than against long-term gains taxed at 12.5%. That leaves ₹15,000 of short-term gains. His ₹20,000 crypto loss can be set off against nothing at all, not even his Bitcoin gain.

body.title: His Long-Term Equity Tax
body.prompt: Aarav's long-term equity gains are ₹1,80,000 from shares plus ₹60,000 from funds. After the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption, what is his tax at 12.5%, before cess, in rupees?
body.explanation: Total long-term equity gains are ₹2,40,000. After the ₹1,25,000 exemption, ₹1,15,000 is taxable, and 12.5% of that is ₹14,375. The exemption applies once to the combined figure, not separately to shares and funds.

children.text: Step 3: The Plot, Computed Both Ways

body.title: Full Working for the Plot Sale

content.caption: Plot bought FY 2015-16 for ₹18,00,000, sold for ₹42,00,000 in FY 2026-27, with ₹10,00,000 invested in section 85 bonds

children.text: He is a resident individual who bought the plot before 23 July 2024, so he pays the lower of the two: ₹87,348. The bonds must be bought within six months of the sale and held for five years, and the ₹50 lakh annual cap comfortably covers his ₹10,00,000.

body.caption: Aarav's tax for tax year 2026-27 (new regime, surcharge not applicable at this income level)

cells: Plot, after bonds exemption, lower of the two methods

body.label: Tax on His Capital Gains Alone
body.context: Before cess, and excluding the slab tax on his salary, debt fund gain and US stock gain. His total tax for the year is ₹3,25,492 including cess.

children.text: Step 5: What He Should Have Done Differently

body.title: Aarav's Missed Opportunities
body.scenario: Looking back at the year, Aarav sees four decisions he made without thinking about tax: selling US stocks at 14 months, holding crypto positions that produced a ₹20,000 loss he could not use, redeeming equity fund units that triggered a short-term loss, and leaving the plot sale tax until filing time.
body.prompt: Which of these could he have handled better, and how?
body.modelAnswer: The US stock sale is the clearest. Foreign shares need more than 24 months, so waiting ten more months would have moved that ₹80,000 gain from his 30% slab to 12.5%, saving roughly ₹14,000 before cess. The crypto loss cannot be rescued: no set-off is allowed, so the only lesson is to size crypto positions knowing losses give no relief. The short-term loss on fund units was actually useful, because he applied it against 20% short-term gains rather than 12.5% long-term ones. The plot sale needed advance tax: the tax on it should have been paid in the instalment following the sale, not at filing, or he would face interest at 1% a month. He could also have checked before 31 March whether booking more unrealised losses, or harvesting gains within the ₹1.25 lakh exemption in a year when he had room, would help.

events.date: Within a week of each sale
events.title: Compute the tax
events.description: Especially for the plot, where the tax runs into lakhs and the instalment deadline follows quickly.

events.title: Pay tax on the gain
events.description: The concession removes interest for earlier instalments, but only if he pays by the instalment following the sale, or 31 March.

events.date: Within 6 months of the plot sale
events.title: Buy the section 85 bonds
events.description: Miss this window and the exemption is gone permanently.

events.title: Review losses and the exemption
events.description: Decide whether to book more losses, and whether any of the ₹1.25 lakh exemption is unused.

events.title: Collect statements and reconcile
events.description: Broker tax P&L, MF Central statement, US broker report, crypto trade history, plot documents, then match against the AIS.

events.title: File ITR-2 and e-verify
events.description: Schedule CG for the gains, Schedule 112A for grandfathered equity, Schedule VDA for crypto and Schedule FA for the US holdings.

body.text: Notice how little of Aarav's tax came from the rates themselves. The big swings came from which clock each asset was on, whether a loss could be used, whether an exemption was claimed in time, and when the tax was paid. That is the whole course in one sentence.

body.title: The One Loss He Could Not Use
body.textWithBlank: Aarav's ₹20,000 loss on Solana could not be set off against anything, because losses on ___ assets get no relief at all.
body.explanation: Losses on virtual digital assets cannot be set off against gains on other tokens, against any other income, or carried forward to later years.

body.title: The Whole Course in Six Cards

cards.definition: A capital gain needs a capital asset and a transfer. No transfer, no tax, however much the value has risen.
12 months for listed securities, 24 months for everything else, with some assets always short-term.
20% short-term and 12.5% long-term for listed equity, 12.5% long-term elsewhere, slab rate for short-term on most other assets.
₹1.25 lakh a year on long-term listed equity gains, applied after losses and before the basic exemption adjustment.
Short-term losses are flexible, long-term losses are not, crypto losses are useless, and carry forward needs on-time filing.
Six months for bonds, the next instalment for advance tax, 31 March for harvesting and the due date for the return.

body.title: Run Your Own Year Through This Sequence
steps: List every sale, redemption, switch, buyback, maturity and crypto transfer in the tax year
Put each into its bucket: short-term or long-term, and at which rate
Set off losses, applying flexible short-term losses against the most heavily taxed gains
Apply the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, then any unused basic exemption if you are a resident with low other income
Claim reinvestment exemptions only where the deadlines and lock-ins are met
Pay advance tax by the instalment following each large sale, then file on time and e-verify

points: Classification comes before computation: the clock and the rate are decided asset by asset
A short-term loss is best applied against the most heavily taxed gains, and crypto losses cannot be used at all
Residents selling pre-July 2024 property should always compute tax both ways and pay the lower
Reinvestment exemptions and harvesting only work inside their deadlines
Foreign shares follow the 24-month clock, which catches many investors who assume 12 months
The final number depends less on the headline rates than on timing, set-off and paperwork
